p.seg: *Féng Yù Piān* (Chapter on Fortuitous Encounters)
*Cāoxíng* (moral conduct) has constant worth,
official careers have inconstant encounters.
Whether one is worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent;
whether one encounters opportunity or not
is a matter of time.
High talent and pure conduct
cannot guarantee certain honor and nobility;
meager abilities and sullied morals
cannot guarantee certain baseness and lowliness.
Perhaps those with high talent and pure conduct,
If not encountered (by a ruler),
To be relegated to the lower stream;
With meager ability, to muddy one's integrity;
To be favored,
is to be above the masses.
Each age has its own way of selecting scholars,
and scholars also each have their own way of advancing.
Advancement depends on favor,
retreat depends on lack of favor.
To occupy a position of honor and prominence
does not necessarily mean one is virtuous,
it is due to being favored;
to be in a humble position below
does not necessarily mean one is foolish,
it is due to lack of favor.
Therefore, when favored,
one might embrace corrupt conduct
and be more respected than in the court of Jié:
When not favored,
one might uphold pure integrity
and be lower than in the court of Yáo.
The reasons for being favored or not favored
are not uniform:
Sometimes one is truly virtuous but assists evil;
sometimes one uses great talent to follow lesser talent;
sometimes both have great talent, but their paths differ in purity;
sometimes one lacks morals but is suitable due to their skills;
sometimes one lacks skills but gains favor due to their beauty.
Wǔ Yuán, Bó Xǐ,
both served Fūchāi.
Bó Xǐ was respected,
Wǔ Yuán was executed.
This is a case of different conduct under the same ruler.
Or, there are cases of the same conduct under different rulers,
with varying fortune,
Yī Yǐn and Jī Zǐ are examples of this.
Yī Yǐn and Jī Zǐ, their talents were the same,
Yī Yǐn became prime minister,
Jī Zǐ became a slave;
Yī Yǐn met Chéng Tāng,
Jī Zǐ met Shāng Zhòu.
When a worthy serves a worthy ruler,
and the ruler desires to govern well,
the minister assists him with his talent,
their tendencies and preferences coinciding,
their success is naturally appropriate.
When a worthy serves an evil ruler,
and the ruler does not desire to govern well,
the minister assists him with loyal conduct,
their conduct and ambitions clashing,
their failure is naturally appropriate.
Or, sometimes a worthy and sage minister
encounters a ruler who desires to govern well,
yet ultimately meets with misfortune,
Kǒngzǐ and Mèng Kē are examples of this.
Kǒngzǐ ran out of provisions in Chén and Cài,
Mèng Kē was stuck in Qí and Liáng.
It's not that the rulers of those times did not want to use good men,
but that their talent and knowledge were shallow,
and they were unable to employ great talents.
For the one who can control excellent steeds,
must be Wang Liang;
those who can employ Yu, Ji, and Gao Yao as ministers,
must be Yao and Shun.
Using a hand capable of maneuvering within a hundred *li*,
to control feet capable of traveling a thousand *li*,
there will inevitably be the danger of breaking the yoke and snapping the harness;
having the talent to manage common subjects,
and using it to control the wisdom of great ministers,
there will inevitably be a transformation of closed minds and blocked intentions.
Therefore, the most profound words are discarded,
and sages and worthies are resisted,
not because they are hated,
but because the profound words are unpalatable.
Sages and worthies strive for loftiness,
and profound words are difficult to put into practice.
Now, when great talent tries to interact with small talent,
the small talent cannot accept it,
so it is only natural that it is not encountered/accepted.
Or, when a minister of great talent,
encounters a ruler of great talent,
there can still be instances of being encountered or not encountered.
Yú Shùn, Xǔ Yóu, Tàigōng, and Bó Yí are examples of this.
Yú Shùn and
Xǔ Yóu were both sages.
They both lived during the Táng dynasty,
and both were presented before Yáo.

and employed six domestic thieves,
who killed Huá Wú with pī-spears behind the zuǒshī (Left Commander) of Sòng at Hé.
The zuǒshī was afraid and said:
"This old man is innocent."
Afterwards, the zuǒshī resented Huáchén,

Huáchén thought that the zuǒshī had come to attack him,

Huáchén himself killed Huá Wú, yet the zuǒshī was afraid;

The fear of King Chéng,

The thunder and rain arrived,

Those who believe in destiny say:
"Knowing oneself is auspicious,

If heaven's mandate is auspicious and generous,
it will be obtained without seeking;

If things grow on their own without being sought,
then there are also people who become noble on their own without seeking nobility.
In human nature, there are those who become good on their own without being taught,
and there are those who, even when taught, never become good,
innate nature is like destiny.
The King Yì of Yuè fled into the mountains,
sincerely unwilling [to be king],
hoping to find a replacement himself.
The people of Yuè smoked him out of his cave,
so he could not escape,
and they forcibly installed him as their ruler.
And the mandate of Heaven is inevitable;
even if one tries to escape it,
one ultimately cannot depart from it.
Therefore, isn't it noble for a man not to seek but to attain it naturally?
"On Qi and Longevity"
Ordinary people's appointed fates are of two kinds:
first, the fate of what one is destined to encounter;
second, the fate of strength and weakness, longevity and premature death.
What one is destined to encounter
refers to death by weapons, burning, crushing, or drowning;
strength and longevity, weakness and premature death
refer to the thickness or thinness of the qi one is endowed with.
Death by weapons, burning, crushing, or drowning depends on the endowment one has as fate;
there is necessarily no fixed time for it.
As for strength and weakness, premature death and longevity, a hundred is taken as the standard;
those who do not reach a hundred
are naturally deficient in qi.
If the endowment of qi is thick, then the body is strong;
if the body is strong, then its lifespan is long;
if the qi is thin, then the body is weak;
if the body is weak, then its lifespan is short;
if the lifespan is short, then there are many illnesses
and short lifespans.
Dying shortly after birth,
or being injured before delivery,
is due to a thin and weak endowment;
people with a thick and strong endowment will certainly complete their allotted lifespan.
As for those who have no encounters,
live idly in impoverished conditions,
and die of shortness of breath,
this is because their endowment is thin
and they have exhausted its use.
